question: Kofola vznikla v Československu z výskumu, ktorý hľadal využitie pre prebytočný kofeín. Pri pražení čoho tento kofeín zostával?
source_excerpt: Kofola originated in the Czechoslovak Research Institute of Medicinal Plants in Prague in 1959

extra.why_interesting: Slovaks see Kofola as the 'socialist Coca-Cola', a cola copy. In fact it grew out of coffee research, so the national soft drink is really a child of coffee. Players can reason their way there from the caffeine and the 'Kofo-' sound without the stem saying it.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia states Kofola originated in 1959 from research using surplus caffeine from coffee roasting, so 'Kávy' is correct (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kofola).

explanation: Sirup Kofo, základ Kofoly, vyvinuli z kofeínu, ktorý zostával pri pražení kávy. Náš najslávnejší limonádový symbol je teda vlastne vedľajší produkt kávy.

question: Slovenské slovo „čaj“ a anglické „tea“ znejú úplne inak, a predsa obe pochádzajú z toho istého jazyka. Z ktorého?
source_excerpt: Both words come from Chinese, though through different routes: Cha via Cantonese, Tea via Min Chinese tê.

extra.why_interesting: Players assume 'čaj' and 'tea' are unrelated words from different languages, perhaps Russian versus English. In fact both come from Chinese. They sound different because one travelled overland by caravan and the other by ship from a different Chinese dialect.
extra.verification_notes: Both 'čaj' (cha, northern Chinese) and 'tea' (Min Chinese tê via Dutch) derive from Chinese varieties, per https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tea#Etymology.

explanation: Naše „čaj“ putovalo z čínskeho „ča“ po súši cez Perziu, Turecko a Rusko. Anglické „tea“ priviezli holandskí moreplavci z prímorskej provincie Fu-ťien, kde sa čaju hovorí „te“.
